parts.passage:
The Brassica Family: One Plant, Many Vegetables

How one wild coastal plant became cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale and more

Many people are surprised to learn that cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi all belong to the same plant family. Although these vegetables differ greatly in appearance, taste and texture, they all originated from a single wild plant called Brassica oleracea. This species, commonly known as wild cabbage or wild mustard, has grown naturally along the rocky coastlines of Europe for thousands of years. Through careful human selection, it has gradually developed into many of the vegetables that are commonly found in supermarkets today.

The transformation of Brassica oleracea did not happen by chance. It was the result of a process known as selective breeding, in which farmers repeatedly chose plants with desirable characteristics and used them to produce the next generation. Unlike modern genetic engineering, selective breeding does not involve changing a plant’s DNA in a laboratory. Instead, it relies on naturally occurring genetic variation that already exists within a species.

Early farmers noticed that some wild Brassica plants had larger leaves, thicker stems or more compact flower buds than others. By saving seeds only from these preferred plants, they gradually increased the frequency of these characteristics over many generations. As a result, different vegetables began to emerge. Cabbage was developed for its large terminal leaves, broccoli for its flower buds, cauliflower for its undeveloped flower clusters, Brussels sprouts for its side buds, kale for its loose leaves and kohlrabi for its swollen stem.

Although these vegetables look very different, scientists have discovered that they are genetically very similar. Because they all belong to the same species, they are still capable of interbreeding under suitable conditions. This close genetic relationship explains why plant breeders can continue to develop new varieties with improved qualities, such as better taste, higher nutritional value or greater resistance to disease.

The Brassica family is also well known for its impressive nutritional benefits. Most Brassica vegetables contain large amounts of vitamins C and K, dietary fibre and important minerals such as potassium and calcium. They also contain natural plant chemicals called glucosinolates, which give these vegetables their distinctive flavour. When a Brassica vegetable is cut or chewed, these compounds are converted into other substances that may help protect the body from certain diseases. Although researchers continue to investigate these effects, many health experts recommend eating a variety of Brassica vegetables as part of a balanced diet.

However, growing Brassica crops presents several challenges for farmers. Because many members of the family are closely related, they are vulnerable to similar insects and plant diseases. One of the most serious problems is clubroot disease, which attacks the roots and reduces plant growth. Farmers often reduce these risks by rotating crops, improving soil conditions and developing resistant varieties through breeding programmes.

Modern plant scientists now combine traditional breeding methods with advanced genetic techniques. By studying the DNA of Brassica plants, researchers can identify genes responsible for useful characteristics such as drought tolerance, faster growth or resistance to pests. This knowledge enables breeders to produce improved crops more efficiently while still relying on natural breeding methods. Scientists are also preserving wild Brassica populations because they contain valuable genetic diversity that may help future crops adapt to climate change and new diseases.

The history of the Brassica family demonstrates the remarkable influence of human agriculture on plant evolution. From one wild coastal plant, centuries of careful selection have produced a wide range of vegetables with different shapes, colours and uses. Today, Brassica crops are grown throughout the world and play an important role in both human nutrition and global agriculture. Their development provides a clear example of how small genetic differences, guided by human choice, can create extraordinary diversity while maintaining a common biological origin.

parts.passage:
Antarctic Architecture: Halley VI

Inspired by science fiction, the Halley VI Research Station has a lot to teach about how architecture can impact psychology

A One morning in 2004, Hugh Broughton was listening to the radio when two voices caused him to pay attention. One of them he recognised through his work as an architect. It was the President of the Royal Institute of British Architects, George Ferguson. The other was less familiar: the director of the British Antarctic Survey, Chris Rapley. The two were announcing a competition to design a new research station in Antarctica. It was a job, they explained, that presented an unusual set of challenges. The site of the new structure was on floating ice 50 kilometres from the Antarctic mainland. Previous stations built in the vicinity had recorded temperatures as low as -50 degrees Celsius and winds of up to 160 kilometres an hour. Only one had escaped the fate of being completely engulfed by snow and abandoned. But it too was now in jeopardy. Ferguson and Rapley listed a number of criteria that they’d be looking for: a background in building in remote locations, knowledge of extreme climates, and an understanding of complex logistics. Broughton ticked zero of those boxes, but that didn’t prevent him from entering the competition – and winning it.

B The structure that Broughton designed, which was completed in 2012, is called Halley VI. It’s made of eight conjoined pods, raised above the snow by hydraulic legs at the feet of which is a set of massive skis, allowing the entire station to be moved by bulldozers. It doesn’t surprise Broughton that people often use film references to describe his creation. He openly admits that science fiction from the 1960s was a big influence. Of course, a few of Broughton’s ideas had to be tempered when he learned more about the challenges associated with building near the South Pole. He realised that, in a year, only the 12 weeks of summer were suitable for construction work, meaning most of the base had to be prefabricated in South Africa, transported by ship and then built over a few summer seasons. No single element could weigh more than 9 tonnes, lest it fall through the ice during transportation. There was also the matter of complying with the Antarctic Treaty, which governs all activity on the icy continent. The rule outlawing the introduction of any non-indigenous plant life, for example, meant that plans to plant salad vegetables in a garden in the station had to be abandoned.

C Still, Broughton managed to navigate these challenges and enlisted the help of a colour expert to devise a palette that was bright, but not overpowering. Lebanese cedar, which gives off a natural fragrance, was used around parts of the station to combat sensory deprivation. As well, Broughton worked with a team to develop special lighting that simulates the sun’s rhythms; the aim was to mitigate seasonal affective disorder (winter depression) during the 105 days a year in which there is no daylight. Few appreciate the impact of these innovations more than Tom Welsh, Halley VI’s winter station leader. ‘During the winter, you can’t really get out of the station very much,’ he says. ‘So you really rely on getting your mental stimulus from inside the station.’ The large central module is key for this function. It’s where staff meet to watch movies, eat and play pool. Welsh’s team has even constructed a small mini golf course there.

D Life at Halley VI isn’t all fun and games. There’s also the job of conducting research into topics ranging from space weather to ozone levels. Some of this work is done on a purpose-built observation deck atop the northernmost module. The station’s triple-glazed windows and heating system normally keep the temperature fairly moderate, but they’re not completely foolproof. In 2014, a power outage left the entire station exposed to record low temperatures for 19 hours. It was so cold that when someone threw a cup of boiling water in the air, it instantly turned into a cloud of ice crystals.

E Thankfully, the entire crisis was eventually brought under control, and no one was hurt. But it gave Halley VI’s team a taste of what life was like for pioneering Antarctic explorers at the start of the 20th century. Back then, research stations provided the bare essentials of survival. They were usually dirty, stuffy places, where tempers flared and the divisions in ranks were strictly maintained. ‘There were definitely a lot of people living in very close contact with each other,’ says Pip Cheshire, a New Zealand architect who has helped restore a number of old Antarctic huts. ‘There are a few cases of explorers actually succumbing to “cabin fever” in these harsh surroundings.’

F It’s difficult to imagine such bleakness on Halley VI. Here, every measure is taken to make its crew comfortable. Broughton is now seen as an expert in designing research bases, and was commissioned to design a new facility for the Spanish Antarctic programme. NASA also reached out for guidance on how to build stations for long-range space missions. ‘They’ve asked questions like, “How small were the sleeping quarters and what features did you introduce to give them individual personality?”’ he says. ‘They’re interested in how architecture can contribute to psychological wellbeing during long periods of isolation.’

G For Sam Jacob, a London-based architect and writer who recently wrote a foreword for a book about Antarctic architecture, applying Broughton’s ideas to space travel makes sense. ‘Antarctica is the place on Earth that is the least like Earth, if you know what I mean – it’s the place most like another planet,’ he says. ‘So, with that in mind, you can really imagine Halley sitting on a planet in outer space. It’s something that’s not only informed by science fiction, but could also give an idea of how we might actually colonise other places.’

parts.passage:
Lawrence Johnston and Hidcote Garden

Robin Lane Fox writes about the American genius behind a remarkable garden in the English Cotswolds

A Today, the National Trust in the UK administers hundreds of public gardens, while sixty years ago there was only one, Hidcote Manor near the English village of Chipping Campden. In 1949 Hidcote attracted a mere 600 visitors and took all of £30 during its first public season. Nowadays, Hidcote is famous worldwide as a masterpiece of design and planting, attracting 150,000 visitors and raising nearly £1 million from entrance tickets annually.

B Hidcote Garden was the creation of an American in Britain, the shy Major Lawrence Johnston, who came to live on the site in 1907 with his widowed mother, Gertrude Winthrop. In some respects Winthrop feared her son’s talents for expensive landscape gardening and never allowed him full access to the family’s funds. Nonetheless, with her inspiration and guidance Johnston started his design in 1908 and brought it to a peak in the early 1930s when he was in his 60s. He may rightly be ranked at this time beside Harold Nicolson and Vita Sackville-West, creators of Sissinghurst, his garden’s only surviving equal.

C In the last years of his life, Johnston placed faith in his head gardener Nancy Lindsay. Lindsay was undoubtedly a skilled plantswoman but she had many other talents as well, including one for taking offence, and she was ill-suited to dealing with her impassioned views. When the National Trust subsequently acquired the garden from Johnston, none of his crucial garden diaries could be found, and some speculated that Lindsay had burned them to hurt her employer. Whatever their actual fate, Trust gardener Graham Thomas was tasked with reviving Hidcote, and he had to manage without these crucial documents. Thomas knew that for the gardens to be a commercial success he needed to extend those areas that were of most interest to the general public, so he introduced new plants and a Mediterranean Bank where Johnston had had nothing of the sort, while retaining the existing superb structure of avenues and evergreen rooms. As a result, since 1949, the visiting public has innocently been admiring Thomas’s flower plantings, not Johnston’s own. When the important designer Russell Page had visited Hidcote in 1934 he had hailed the half-hardy plants in the summer house as one of the highlights. But Thomas later got rid of them and pulled the house down, fearing such relatively colourless exhibits would not capture the public’s imagination.

D Then, in 2002, Johnston’s old diaries and notebooks resurfaced. The present head gardener had started to give lectures about Hidcote’s lost early designs, during which he appealed for memories from his audience. A few months later an envelope arrived. There was no letter inside, only Johnston’s personal diaries from the 1920s and 30s. The sender may be unknown but the importance of these documents to Hidcote is certain, for they contain invaluable notes regarding the selection of plants and, even better still, detailed sketches by Johnston himself showing how the different parts of the garden are related and how those relationships evolve over the seasons. These documents are a rarity in other ways too, for they never dwell on the issues so typically addressed in diaries – relationships, loves and longings. These are far more interesting, for they represent a classic social history of an English country house during the inter-war years.

E On page after page Johnston describes the layout of the plants and gardens, interspersed, for example, with that day’s guests. The famous novelist Edith Wharton is recorded as coming for lunch, beside a recipe for poison to kill garden weeds. It is this mix of glamour and the everyday that makes the diaries of such peculiar fascination. At their heart, though, these are useful documents containing, for example, lengthy lists of those who might one day be of service around the estate, including local stone masons and glaziers, or repairers of broken china from as far away as France.

F The discovery of the diaries has offered Hidcote a new direction for the years ahead. Inspired by them, an anonymous American has given the gardens £1.6 million. This is a remarkable chance, which the Trust has gladly seized upon to allow for crucial repair work on paths and the famous pool, together with the reconstruction of the old summer house. However, the real implications of the discoveries made from the diaries are more problematic, for now the Trust must take its collection of plants up one notch. We now possess information about the very plants that most appealed to Johnston in the garden’s golden years. Today, these may not be easy to source, nor so appealing to contemporary tastes.

G ‘But isn’t it all so long ago?’, a non-gardening academic recently asked me. On the contrary, Hidcote is still with us, a living legacy. It includes the greatest central vista in British gardening, the design I regard as the greatest in British art in the past century. It was the work of an American genius building an un-American garden of his own. I do not believe the fashionable guess nowadays that Johnston was informed by books on contemporary design by Britain’s Thomas Mawson, an altogether less innovative mind. This is not least because there is so much in the garden to remind us of how Johnston had travelled widely in Europe, which Mawson had not. It is Johnston’s own origins, the events of his life, and his individual design flair that contribute to making Hidcote so unique.
